reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is an instructional walkthrough showing how to register and configure security and identity-verification features on an FTX exchange account. It promotes using a registration link and discount, but the observable requests are ordinary account credentials, two-factor authentication setup, and KYC documents rather than a deceptive promise of guaranteed returns or a request to send money to the creator. The content appears to teach account setup rather than report on or solicit participation in a fraudulent scheme.

opening.argument: The central inducement is a fee benefit tied directly to taking action: viewers are told that clicking the link below will provide a discount, while the walkthrough then requires creating an account with an email address and password. The on-screen registration panel likewise displays a referral code marked as a fee reduction beside the sign-up fields. That is a concrete reward-for-registration pathway, not merely general information about cryptocurrency. Because the promised benefit is attached to an external click and account creation, the presentation functions as a low-barrier acquisition offer that warrants scam treatment.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an instructional walkthrough does not remove the solicitation. The title foregrounds registration and a trading-fee discount, and the speaker expressly connects the discount to clicking a link. The fact that the requested inputs resemble ordinary sign-up fields does not establish that the linked offer is safe or that viewers receive the advertised benefit. The argument also understates that the viewer is being steered toward participation, not simply shown a neutral interface.

The cited fields show ordinary registration inputs, and the walkthrough does not establish that viewers must send money to the presenter or that the link is deceptive. A referral incentive can explain the promotion without converting an account tutorial into a scam.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: an external-link instruction, a discount claim, unusually different discount figures, and a cryptocurrency account flow that collects credentials and identity documentation. The title says “5% Trading Fee Discount,” while the spoken offer says “15 percent off,” creating a material inconsistency in the promised benefit. The walkthrough also proceeds from email and password entry to identity proof and authentication setup. Even without proving a loss, that combination makes the reward-and-registration pitch look like a potentially deceptive acquisition funnel rather than a reliably explained offer.

It calls identity verification routine, yet that verification is part of the same link-driven onboarding sequence.
